Can I ask why this will only be for directional lights?
Is there a limitation in Bend Studio's method that prevents it from being implemented for other light sources?

> Can I ask why this will only be for directional lights? Is there a limitation in Bend Studio's method that prevents it from being implemented for other light sources?

Technically the Bend Studio approach works with all light sources, but the way that it is implemented is more beneficial for Directional lights than for other light types. 

On our end, it is a lot simpler and more efficient to implement it only for directional lights. Directional lights are more stable over time, and its rare to have more than 1 or 2 (and the absolute max is 8), which means that we don't have to do any clever tricks to manage the atlas. Positional lights are constantly shuffled around the atlas, and there can be dozens of shadows positional lights in a scene. 

Ultimately the problem this solves is more urgent for DirectionalLights as well. It is much more feasible to tune positional lights bias to avoid peterpanning and light leakage than it is for directional lights. 

At some point in the future we could consider adding support for contact shadows to positional lights. But I wouldn't do it right now

Hello,

I've been using this PR in my project, and it's been working amazingly well. I absolutely love it.

I did notice one small issue, though. I'm not sure whether it's an oversight, intended behavior, or simply a limitation of the technique. For example, imagine there's a wall between an object and the sun. If I turn the wall's "Cast Shadow" property to off, the regular shadow is removed as expected, but a contact shadow is still cast whenever the wall is in view.

Not sure if this help but if I set the wall's material transparency to 99.9%, the contact shadow is no longer rendered.

Is this expected behavior, or could this be a bug?

Hallo, glad you like it!

This is a known limitation of the technique, sadly. If something is visible on the screen (depth buffer) it will cast a shadow, regardless of other settings. I'd need to double check but I believe what happens when the material is 99.9% transparent is that it is also getting culled by the engine and therefore not drawn to the screen.
Transparent objects don't appear in the depth buffer so that's why they don't show in screen space shadows

The effect appears to be super cheap so that's great. On RTX 5080, it's a mere 0.05 ms. On 9950x3D's APU, it takes around 3 ms to execute, but the whole frame is a whopping 100 ms so the real impact is like 3% of the frame time, which is pretty good.

> Did some tests in Nuku Warriors to see if I could reduce the range of directional shadows, and use SSCS for out of range areas, but nothing really gave good results. 

For long-range dynamic shadows, a SDF/voxel shadow solution integrated in SDFGI/HDDAGI/VoxelGI would be a better fit than contact shadows. They would be less precise, but more stable as they wouldn't depend on screen-space information.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7590 could also help if you can dedicate one of the shadow splits to long-distance shadowing.

Singular directional light case seems to be hitting the new texture type validation checks on master, since `create_texture` creates it as a regular 2D texture, while the uniform set is always expecting an array. It seems this always caused Vulkan validation errors too.

You could fix it by using `create_texture_from_format` to explicitly create it as a 2D array texture.

Edit: Hm, then that triggers validation in SCSS shader because `get_texture_slice_view` returns itself as it detects the slice being identical to the parent texture despite the types being different. This needs some work upstream.

Edit 2: Please check the PR I made on your fork https://github.com/Rudolph-B/godot/pull/1

> I've checked contact shadows in Unity HDRP, the contact shadows won't show on the backface of mesh with translucent materials.

It should work with the Opaque Pre-pass transparency mode in BaseMaterial3D, or alpha scissor/hash since these write to the depth buffer.

> > I've checked contact shadows in Unity HDRP, the contact shadows won't show on the backface of mesh with translucent materials.
> 
> It should work with the Opaque Pre-pass transparency mode in BaseMaterial3D, or alpha scissor/hash since these write to the depth buffer.

In the case of alpha scissor for foliage, I consider proper behaviour that SSCS *not* apply shadows to surfaces that are affected by back lighting.

This is consistent with how shadowmaps currently work, and is necessary so that foliage with SSCS actually looks like foliage, rather than steel sheets in the shape of plants/trees.

I noticed that the shadow opacity parameter in **Light3D** also affects contact shadows, which raises a few questions. Is this intentional? Would it be better to have a dedicated opacity parameter specifically for contact shadows? Also, I'm not sure if keeping the **directional_shadow_allow_contact_shadows** property exclusive to directional lights is the best approach. I believe this property should be in **Light3D**, given that this is supposed to be implemented for positional lights as well. Here's an illustration:

> I noticed that the shadow opacity parameter in Light3D also affects contact shadows, which raises a few questions. Is this intentional?

I don't know about intentionality, but it seems like reasonable behaviour to me. If I'm lowering shadow opacity on a light, I don't want to have parts of the shadows change and others not.

> Would it be better to have a dedicated opacity parameter specifically for contact shadows?

Well, the question then becomes, what use cases are there for having different opacity between shadowmap shadows and SSCS?

If it is added though, maybe SSCS opacity could be handled kinda like PCSS (directional light size) already is. That is, if the value is not zero, the feature (PCSS/SSCS) is enabled, if it's zero, it's considered as disabled.

> Well, the question then becomes, what use cases are there for having different opacity between shadowmap shadows and SSCS?
> 
> If it is added though, maybe SSCS opacity could be handled kinda like PCSS (directional light size) already is. That is, if the value is not zero, the feature (PCSS/SSCS) is enabled, if it's zero, it's considered as disabled.

The only engine I know that does this is Unreal, with the properties "Contact Shadow Casting Intensity" and "Contact Shadow Non Casting Intensity", but I don't know why are there.

A way to handle SSCS opacity could be to make it multiplicative with normal opacity, if it is 50% it will be 50% of whatever normal shadow opacity is. This I think would at least keep be an expected way to link behaviour between them for the user.

I have serious doubts about whether it's correct for the **contact shadows** property to be a subgroup of **shadow**. While this might make sense for directional lights, it doesn't for positional lights, since contact shadows can be used as a replacement for shadow maps as they tend to be cheaper.

> I have serious doubts about whether it's correct for the **contact shadows** property to be a subgroup of **shadow**. While this might make sense for directional lights, it doesn't for positional lights, since contact shadows can be used as a replacement for shadow maps as they tend to be cheaper.

The idea here is to only support _contact shadows_ (i.e. shadows intended to bridge the gap between the mesh and the shadows from shadow maps). Having full scale screen space shadows as a replacement for shadow maps is way out of scope, and is not something that we are planning on supporting. 

IMO I don't think raw screen space shadows are a good fit for a general purpose engine, the only case where they can replace shadow maps are when:
1. Your light range is very small, and
2. The user can never get close to the light (i.e. the range in screen space is also small). 

If a light's range ever covers a significant portion of the screen, screen space shadows will slow down significantly. They are nice when you have highly dynamic content and a fixed camera. But for a general purpose engine, I don't think they will ever be a good fit. Keep in mind, you can't cache screen space shadows, so you pay the full cost of the trace every frame for every visible pixel. With shadow maps, they are cached automatically, so they are generally extremely cheap in comparison
